Captured live from MAME's debugger console through the gdbstub, on the 68000 board of
m68k-dual, the machine stopped in the debugger.
Program and board names were then replaced by neutral labels by a single mechanical substitution
that preserves every field width; nothing else was edited.

dasm.txt        the FILE written by `dasm <scratch>/dasm.txt,0,10` (address 0, 0x10 = 16 BYTES)
dasm.reply.txt  what the console answered to that command
find.txt        `find 0,10000,00,20,10,00` (the reference image's first four bytes, over the first 64 KB)
find.none.txt   `find 0,10000,de,ad,be,ef,ca,fe` (a pattern that is not there)
history.txt     `history ,8` after twelve single steps from reset

The parsers in server.py are written against these bytes, never against a shape authored from
memory; a change in MAME's output is re-captured here, not patched in the fixture.

The captures above were typed with BARE numbers. The tools send the same commands with the `0x`
prefix on every number (`dasm dasm.txt,0x0,0x10`, `find 0x0,0x10000,0x00,0x20,0x10,0x00`,
`history ,0x8`), because MAME's expression parser reads a bare `d0` as the D0 register; the
prefixed spellings were proven on the same board through the tools themselves, answering the
same five lines, the same two hits and the same eight-line trail.

Captured live through the `disassemble` TOOL (the `lines` of its reply, which are the
non-empty lines of the file the console's `dasm` wrote), on the v30-alt board,
the machine stopped in the debugger, `bases={"DATA": "400"}`:

dasm.v30.new_irq_video.txt   `disassemble(ref="new_irq_video", length=48)`: a routine with
                             DIRECT memory operands (`word ptr [0C014h]`, `[0E849h]`), which
                             the listing prints as the raw offset inside the DATA class and
                             not as the linear address (`0x400 + offset`) `read_memory` and
                             `watch_add` take; `symbols_find(linear="c414")` answered
                             `IN_IRQ + 0` and `linear="ec49"` `TOTALTIME + 0` on the same board.
                             It also holds the shapes that are NOT direct operands: an
                             immediate (`mov aw,40h`), a branch target (`bne 0F5BD1h`) and
                             call targets (`call 0FD108h`).
dasm.v30.startdemo.txt       `disassemble(ref="startdemo", length=48)`: the register-relative
                             shapes that must not be resolved (`ds1:[bw-31BBh]`, `ps:[ix]`,
                             `[ix]`) and an immediate (`0CA35h`), beside the one direct
                             operand of the listing (`byte ptr [0CA34h]`).

Captured live through `mame_read.dasm_lines`, the same range written twice, WITH the opcode
bytes (`dasm dasm.txt,<addr>,<len>`) and WITHOUT them (`dasm dasm.bare.txt,<addr>,<len>,0`), the
machine parked at `start`, each file copied verbatim out of the scratch:

dasm.m68k.560.txt               the m68k-dual board, 0x560 for
dasm.m68k.560.bare.txt          0x40 bytes: the tail of an interrupt handler holding a
                                conditional branch (`beq`), a call (`jsr`) and a return (`rte`),
                                the first window from 0x400 up that held all three
dasm.v30.30000.txt              the v30 board, 0x30000 for
dasm.v30.30000.bare.txt         0xb0 bytes: the program's entry, with `br`, `call`, `bc`, `be`,
                                `dbnz`, two `rep`-prefixed string moves and a `reti`; and a text
                                string between 0x3002D and 0x3004F that decodes as instructions,
                                which is what a listing over data looks like

Captured live through `Session.monitor` (the exact text the list parsers receive), on the same
m68k-dual board, the machine stopped in the debugger, each list after a `bpclear` or
`wpclear` sent the same way. MAME's console buffer wraps every line at its `MAX_LINE_LENGTH`
(`src/emu/debug/textbuf.cpp`): at a space when the line has one, dropping the space, and with a
hard cut at the column when it has none. The conditions are `d0==0x<zeros>1`, whose leading
zeros change the length and not the value:

bplist.row249.txt        `bp 400,<c>` sized so the printed row is one short of the wrap column
bplist.row250.txt        the same row AT the wrap column: cut at the space after `if`
bplist.row251.txt        one past it
bplist.at-limit.txt      the condition whose `bp` command is at the stub's packet limit (read
                         off the session's advertised packet size): the header piece, then hard
                         cuts at the column
bplist.space-early.txt   `d0==0x1 || d1==0x<zeros>1`: the last space before the column is early
bplist.space-late.txt    `d0==0x<zeros>1 || d1==0x1`: a space a few columns before the column
bplist.two-rows.txt      the at-limit row, then `bp 404,d0==1` beside it
wplist.cond-short.txt    `wpset 0x2031fc,0x4,w,d0==1`
wplist.cond-wrapped.txt  the same watchpoint under a condition long enough to wrap

Captured live from the console's own stdout (`stdout.log` in the scratch), on the same 68000
m68k-dual board, by the block that went looking for a line nobody answers: a fresh
machine, then twenty repetitions of the sequence measured to kill the console's reader (one
`perform` of `captures`, `screen_signature`, `state_save` under a fresh name, `throttle(off)`,
`resume`, `stop`) with two `read_block` calls at the address map's edges after each. The whole
file as the session wrote it, never sliced:

session.volume.stdout    what `eaten` had no case against: a console log with REAL volume, 82
                         echoed command lines numbered 2..83, each between 463 and 2433 bytes,
                         and ONE reader death sitting among them rather than at either end.
                         Eleven echoes fall before that death and seventy-one after it, which
                         is what lets the discriminating case be asked at all: `eaten` works by
                         finding this line's echo and searching the tail after it, so the claim
                         its docstring makes -- that a report sitting BEFORE this line's echo
                         belongs to somebody else's line -- needs a second candidate somewhere
                         in the buffer, and a double of one or two lines has nowhere to put
                         one. Its SIZE is part of the contract and a test asserts it: a later
                         shrink goes red instead of quietly removing the axis.

The reader's death in that file is the one the console prints STARTING UP (`require`'s
`setcompletion` read as a table), which is the shape measured on this board; the block it came
from did not reproduce the line nobody answers, so nothing here is a capture of that.

Captured live through `Session.monitor`, on the same m68k-dual board, the machine
stopped in the debugger on a fresh start with no registerpoint of anybody's. A registerpoint's
index is printed in HEX (`%X`), the list is newest first, and the condition goes inside braces
because the console reads a bare `d1==7fff` as an assignment:

rpset.unknown-symbol.txt       `rpset {eax==5}`: a register this cpu lacks, and nothing is armed
print.braces.unknown-symbol.txt  `print {eax==5}`: the same refusal from the evaluator
print.braces.malformed.txt     `print {d1==}`: the evaluator refuses what `rpset` ARMS
print.braces.false.txt         `print {d1==7fff}` while D1 holds something else
rpset.malformed-armed.txt      `rpset {d1==}`: MAME arms a condition it cannot evaluate
rplist.two-rows.txt            `rplist` after it: the malformed row ABOVE the first one
rpclear.cleared.txt            `rpclear 2`
rpclear.invalid.txt            `rpclear 7`, a number no row holds
rplist.disabled.txt            `rplist` after `rpdisable 1`: the row keeps a leading `D`
rpset.unknown-command.txt      `rpzzzset {1}`: how this console answers a command it lacks,
                               which is what a debugger with no registerpoints would say
rplist.cond-with-spaces.txt    `rplist` after `rpset {d1==7fff && d0!=0x12345678}`
rpset.sixteenth.txt            the sixteenth `rpset` of a session: `Registerpoint 10 set`
rplist.sixteen.txt             `rplist` after it: `10`, then `F` down to `A`, then `9`
rplist.two-devices.txt         the board has two 68000s: `rpset {d1==7fff}`, `focus subcpu`, the

                               condition text under each, one counter for both

Captured live through `Session.monitor`, same board, `:maincpu` visible, the machine stopped in
the debugger on a fresh start, after `bpclear`, `wpclear` and `rpclear` (each answering `Cleared
all ...points`). An ACTION goes inside braces, as the debugger documentation writes it
(`docs.mamedev.org/debugger`: "you may need to surround the action with braces { } to ensure
commas and semicolons within the command are not interpreted in the context of the ... command
itself"); typed bare, `bp 400,temp1++;g` lost its `;g` to the console (`bplist.by-address.txt`).

the action after `do`, spaces kept as typed, and prints NO `if` for a condition of `1`:

not matched.

Captured the same way (the `debug` tool's `output`, patched build, a fresh start), for a write
watch conditioned on the value it carries. `wpdata`, `wpaddr` and `wpsize` sit in the debugger's
GLOBAL symbol table (`debugcpu.cpp`), so the console evaluates them outside a watchpoint, as 0;
a condition MAME cannot parse at the arm is refused, and one it can parse but not evaluate is
ARMED and never fires (`points.cpp` returns on an `expression_error`), which is why a condition
is put to the evaluator before the `wp`:

Captured through the `debug` TOOL (its `output`), on `circus` (the stock debug build patched for
SDL3's joystick ids, `joystickprovider none`): `print frame,totalcycles` four times, each answer
kept whole and in order, one blank line closing each as the console prints it. MAME's debugger
refreshes `totalcycles` only when the cpu executes, so right after `stateload` it still holds
the count from before the load while `frame` already reads the loaded one:

totalcycles-after-load.txt   after `run_for(frames=10)` and `state_save("c1")`; after
                             `run_for(frames=5)`; after `state_load("c1")` (the loaded frame,
                             the count the machine held at its stop before the load); after
                             one `step` (the loaded count plus that instruction's cycles)

Read off MAME's source rather than captured from a console, at revision
9c28def3407cf3386d5c6bea932312741acb7992 of the MAME checkout the board's build was made from: every
`register_command` call in src/emu/debug/debugcmd.cpp and debugcon.cpp, one per line as `name
minparams maxparams`, the maximum spelled as the source spells it (`MAX_COMMAND_PARAMS`). The
classifier's tables are judged against this list, so a command MAME adds or drops is a red test
rather than a word the tables silently leave unjudged. Regenerated from a checkout's
src/emu/debug with:

    grep -ho 'register_command("[^"]*" *,[^,]*, *[0-9]*, *[A-Z_0-9]*' debugcmd.cpp debugcon.cpp \
      | sed -E 's/register_command\("([^"]*)" *,[^,]*, *([0-9]*), *([A-Z_0-9]*)/\1 \2 \3/'


commands.registered.txt      every registration, in source order

Captured through the `debug` TOOL (its `output`), on `circus` started with an ini holding
`rewind 1`, after `run_for(frames=10)` and `run_for(frames=2)`: `debug("rewind")` with no rewind
state the machine could step back to. It is MAME's own refusal of the command
(`execute_rewind` in src/emu/debug/debugcmd.cpp prints it when `rewind_step` fails, and prints
nothing on success), so the machine was not replaced:

rewind.refused.txt           the console's whole answer, its closing blank line included

Captured from MAME's `error.log`, not its console, on `circus` built from MAME master 285ea99f
with patches 0003 and 0005, whose gdbstub refreshes the display after every console command:
`run_for(frames=10)`, then `state_save`. The refreshes of the console commands before it ran
circus's screen update with the machine stopped, which asserted its IRQ and left the line's
event pending as an anonymous timer, so MAME held the save (`handle_saveload` asks
`device_scheduler::can_save`, which logs this and dumps the timers). Cut from its first line to
the dump's closing rule:

statesave.held.errorlog.txt  MAME's words for a held save, and the timer dump that follows them
